def: The metal tip that touches the paper. A thin slit runs down its middle so ink can flow to the point, and the tines flex slightly as you write.
The comb-shaped part under the nib. It carries ink forward and lets air flow back, so the pen writes steadily instead of gulping or leaking.
The part you hold, between the barrel and the nib. Also called the grip.
The main body of the pen. In some designs it is also the ink tank.
The way liquid creeps through very narrow gaps. It pulls ink along the feed and the nib slit toward the paper.
A refillable ink holder that fits where a cartridge would go. You twist or press it to draw bottled ink into the pen.
A small sealed tube of ink that pushes onto a spike in the section. Easy and clean, but you are limited to the inks that fit.
The barrel itself holds the ink and you fill it with a dropper. It holds a lot, but the threads must be sealed well.
A knob at the end turns a piston up and down inside the barrel to draw ink in. Large capacity and neat.
A plunger or rod changes the pressure inside the barrel so ink is pushed in. It can hold a lot and often shows the ink level.
A small side lever squeezes a rubber ink sac. Release it and the sac draws ink up through the nib.
A button on the end of the barrel presses a bar that squeezes the ink sac.
A soft rubber ink bag inside many older pens. Over the years it hardens and needs replacing.
A filling system by Sheaffer with a thin tube that slides out of the nib end, so the nib itself never goes into the ink.
A squeezable sac inside a metal sleeve, used in Parker pens such as the 51. Pinch the sleeve to fill.
Hardened rubber used for barrels and feeds. It feels warm, but sunlight can turn black ebonite brownish over time.
An early plastic used from the early 1900s. It gave pens bright swirled colours, and it can shrink and crack as it ages.
Modern plastics used for most pens today. They hold bright colours and are stable and light.
A soft nib whose tines spread apart under pressure and make thick and thin lines. Common on older pens and needs a light touch.
Nibs ground flat at the tip. They write thick downstrokes and thin crossstrokes, which gives writing a calligraphic look.
Common names for line width. They are not exact: a Japanese medium is usually thinner than a Western medium.
A tiny bead of very hard metal welded to the end of the nib so that it wears slowly.
A nib mostly covered by the section, so only the tip shows. The Parker 51 made this look famous.
A pen made from clear material so you can see the ink and sometimes the filling mechanism inside.
Ink spreading into little hairs around a line on poor or thin paper.
Ink showing up on the other side of the page.
Changes in darkness inside a single stroke, where thin spots show the ink’s lighter tone.
A coloured shimmer that some inks leave on dried lines, often red or green on blue ink.
A word meaning “of one’s own country”. In early 20th-century India it was applied to pens and inks made at home instead of imported.
The pointed iron stylus used to scratch letters into palm leaves in south India. Soot or oil is rubbed in afterward to make them readable.
